8. Power Series

Inside the radius of convergence — Abel and Tauber theorems, rearrangements, Cauchy products.

  • Power Series and Radius of Convergence — A power series ∑anxn\sum a_n x^n∑an​xn converges absolutely inside its radius RRR and diverges outside — watch three archetypal series pin down their radii, and see why the boundary ∣x∣=R\lvert x\rvert = R∣x∣=R must be decided case by case.
  • Hadamard Gap Theorem — SN(z)=∑k=0Nz2kS_N(z) = \sum_{k=0}^{N} z^{2^k}SN​(z)=∑k=0N​z2k (gap ratio exactly 2): plotting ∣SN(reiθ)∣|S_N(r e^{i\theta})|∣SN​(reiθ)∣ for r∈{0.90,0.95,0.99}r \in \{0.90, 0.95, 0.99\}r∈{0.90,0.95,0.99}, spikes erupt at more and more angles as NNN grows — a gappy series with radius exactly 1 is singular at every point of the unit circle. The gap-free contrast ∑zk/(k+1)2\sum z^k/(k+1)^2∑zk/(k+1)2 stays calm.
  • Abel's Theorem — For a convergent series ∑an→S\sum a_n \to S∑an​→S, the power series ∑anxn\sum a_n x^n∑an​xn approaches SSS as x→1−x \to 1^{-}x→1− — Abel's theorem. Even the divergent Grandi series points to 12\frac{1}{2}21​ in this limit, but that is the Abel sum, never "the sum" of the series.
  • Tauber's Theorem — Grandi's series has Abel sum 12\frac{1}{2}21​ yet diverges — because ∣n an∣=n|n\,a_n| = n∣nan​∣=n breaks the hypothesis an=o(1/n)a_n = o(1/n)an​=o(1/n). The series dn=(−1)n(n+1)ln⁡(n+2)d_n = \frac{(-1)^n}{(n+1)\ln(n+2)}dn​=(n+1)ln(n+2)(−1)n​ satisfies it, and its Abel-sum curve reaches the ordinary sum — Tauber's theorem.
  • Two Roads to e — Compare how fast compound growth (1+1n)n(1+\frac{1}{n})^n(1+n1​)n and the series ∑k=0∞1k!\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k!}∑k=0∞​k!1​ approach eee. The factorial series wins by a landslide.
  • ζ(4) and Even Powers — The partial sums of 1n4\frac{1}{n^4}n41​ reach π490\frac{\pi^4}{90}90π4​ quickly — and at every even power, the ζ\zetaζ value closes into a power of π\piπ.
  • Rearranging Changes the Sum — Reordering a conditionally convergent series changes its sum — ln⁡2≈0.6931\ln 2 \approx 0.6931ln2≈0.6931 becomes 32ln⁡2≈1.0397\frac{3}{2}\ln 2 \approx 1.039723​ln2≈1.0397. Twin of the Leibniz scene.
  • Absolute Convergence — If the absolute-value series converges, so does the original — compare the two partial-sum walks SnS_nSn​ and TnT_nTn​ settling together against the harmonic-like case where the signs rescue a divergent absolute series.
  • Riemann's Rearrangement Theorem — A conditionally convergent series can be rearranged to sum to any real number — watch the greedy block rule steer the alternating harmonic series (which sums to ln⁡2\ln 2ln2 in its natural order) onto a target of your choice.
  • The Cauchy Product — (∑an)(∑bn)=∑cn(\sum a_n)(\sum b_n) = \sum c_n(∑an​)(∑bn​)=∑cn​ with cn=∑k=0nakbn−kc_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k b_{n-k}cn​=∑k=0n​ak​bn−k​ — sweeping the lattice along diagonals. Mertens' theorem (absolute convergence on one side saves the product) and the counterexample when both converge only conditionally.
